name: Kumasi
info: Kumasi is a city in the rain forest of Ghana, about 200 kilometres from Accra, founded around 1680 as the capital of the Ashanti Empire and now the capital of the Ashanti Region and the seat of the Asantehene.

facts.founded: Around 1680, or in the 1680s, by Asantehene Osei Kofi Tutu I as the capital of the Ashanti Empire; oral accounts differ on how the site was chosen.
facts.where: On the eastern slopes of a ridge rising from the marshes of the Nsuben rivers, in a rain forest region near Lake Bosomtwe in the Ashanti Region of Ghana, about 200 kilometres from Accra.
facts.known: Capital of the Ashanti Empire; seat of the Asantehene; the Golden Stool; Okomfo Anokye; the British burnings of 1874 and the siege of 1900; the Kejetia Market; kente cloth
facts.today: Kumasi is the second largest city in Ghana and the capital of the Ashanti Region, and it remains the seat of the Asantehene.

t: Kumasi was founded around 1680 as the capital of the Ashanti Empire, and its ruler, the Asantehene, was also ruler of the empire.
The Aowin sacked the city in 1718 and 1719, and the British burnt parts of it in 1874, invaded it again in 1895 and 1896 and ended the war of 1900 with the defeat of the Ashanti by 1 January 1901.
Under British rule from 1901 the city was modernised with railways, a fort, hospitals and colleges, and after Ghana's independence in 1957 it became the capital of the Ashanti Region.
dyk: According to legend, it was at Kumasi that Okomfo Anokye received the Golden Stool, the embodiment of the soul of the Ashanti nation, and the city's name means "under the kum tree".

sections.origins:
Kumasi stands in a rain forest region of Ghana near Lake Bosomtwe, about 200 kilometres from Accra. The city was built over the eastern slopes of a ridge, rising from the marshes of the Nsuben rivers. Its name comes from the Twi word Kumase, meaning "under the kum tree", and the word was the name of an Okum tree in Kwaman, planted by Okomfo Anokye.

Kumasi was founded around 1680, or in the 1680s, by Asantehene Osei Kofi Tutu I as the capital of the Ashanti Empire. Accounts of its formation differ. One holds that Osei Tutu negotiated for the land under a kum tree. Other oral sources say that Nana Oti Akenten negotiated with the chief of Tafo for a plot of land under a kum tree. Other traditions hold that Oti built Kwaman and that his son Nana Obiri Yeboa created Kumasi instead. The majority of oral sources attribute the choice of site to Okomfo Anokye, who was said to have planted two kum seeds, one in Kwaman and one in Kumawu, and to have decreed that the one that grew would be the capital of Osei Tutu's empire.
sections.growth:
The city rose to prominence in 1695, when it became the capital of the Ashanti Empire under Osei Tutu. After the victory over Denkyira in 1701 the Ashanti empire became the primary state among the Ashanti. Visitors of the 19th century described a large and orderly town. In 1816 Huydecooper wrote of clean and straight streets and houses excellently built, most of them of one storey. In 1817 Thomas Edward Bowdich found that the central city, without suburbs such as Bantama and Asafo, was oblong and about 4 miles round, with four principal streets half a mile long and 50 to 100 yards wide. It had 27 streets then, and another source named 50 by the mid-1880s.

Estimates of the population under the empire vary. In the early 19th century Ashanti sources gave 100,000 and European sources 12,000 to 15,000, and another source of 1820 gave more than 200,000. According to the historian Ivor Wilks the city may have had 40,000 people in the 1860s. Before 1883 there were 150 loggias called dampans in the city. The Great Market, Dwaberem, served as a marketplace, parade ground, royal courthouse and place to receive prominent visitors, and Apremoso, named after cannons captured at the Battle of Feyiase, was where the Asantehene, officials and people could gather.
sections.rulers:
The ruler of Kumasi, the Asantehene, was also ruler of the Ashanti Empire, which at its peak covered large parts of present-day Ghana and the Ivory Coast. Osei Tutu made it the capital, and in 1718 and 1719 Opoku Ware I defended it against the Aowin. The palace complex stood in the eastern quarter of the central city.

The British took parts of the city in 1874 in the Third Anglo-Ashanti War and invaded it again between 1895 and 1896. The state of Ashanti then became a formal colony of the British Empire, and Kumasi was formally annexed in 1901. The Kumasi Public Health Board was established in 1925 as the modern local government. In 1926 the Ashanti king Prempeh I returned after 30 years of exile in the Seychelles, and Kumasi was given ceremonial control over the Ashanti sub-states. The colonial administration restored the full role of king in 1935.

After Ghana gained independence in 1957 Kumasi became the capital of the Ashanti Region. It remains the seat of the Asantehene. In 1988 it was designated a Metropolitan under PNDCL 208, and the Local Government Act of 1993 allowed local assembly representatives to be elected and to take part in planning.
sections.life:
The city had 77 wards, and specific wards were inhabited by a particular class of artisans or workers: goldsmiths, umbrella makers, coffin makers, executioners and city patrollers each lived in their own sections. Bowdich recorded that each street was named and that a superior captain was placed in charge of it. A uniformed police maintained security. He also recorded public toilets on the outskirts of the town and toilets in each house, into which boiling water was poured daily, and the waste of the houses was burned behind the street every morning. In peaceful times the red and white clay of the buildings was regularly polished and renewed.

Muslims from Islamic states in what is now Ghana formed a permanent settlement in Kumasi during the reign of Osei Bonsu. Dupuis recorded about 1000 of them in 1820, and the first Islamic schools of the empire were founded in Kumasi in the early 19th century. Kumasi is the centre of Asante culture, and it is known for kente, a traditional textile.

Under British rule the economy became cash-based, with industries for rubber and cocoa, and 11 European firms were established in 1907. The colonial government removed barriers to migration, and people from the Northern Territories, Syrians, Lebanese and Indians came. Schmidt argues that the colonial government segregated Kumasi's residential districts on racial lines.
sections.crises:
In 1718 and 1719 the Aowin king Ebirimoro invaded Kumasi and sacked the capital while Asantehene Opoku Ware I and his army were away at the front. The Dutch at Axim recorded that the Aowin plundered the city's gold and captured 20,000 of its people, and a number of the city's royals were killed. Opoku Ware was able to beat back the invasion.

In 1874, during the Third Anglo-Ashanti War, the British burnt parts of the city, including the royal residence. Native carriers were generally blamed for torching it, and British engineers made strenuous efforts to put out the fires. A civil war in Asante lasting five years, which ended by 1888, caused further decline. R. Austin Freeman, visiting in 1888, found a large clearing in the forest with scattered groups of houses and wasteland where houses had stood, and wrote that since the destruction of 1874 the people did not seem to have had heart to rebuild them.

Between 1895 and 1896 the British invaded Kumasi again. The Secretary of State for the Colonies justified the expedition by saying it was to appoint a resident in Kumasi who would see that the king carried out his engagements. In 1900 a war broke out after Governor Frederick Mitchell Hodgson made a speech in Kumasi demanding the Golden Stool. The Ashanti held Hodgson under siege in the fort until he broke out of the city on 23 June 1900, and British war operations ended on 1 January 1901 with the defeat of the Ashanti. By 1901 the population had declined to 3000.
sections.legacy:
Kumasi holds an important place in the history of the Ashanti people. Legend claims that it was here that Okomfo Anokye received the Golden Stool, the embodiment of the soul of the Ashanti nation. Royal Asante sites in the city include the Manhyia Palace, dating from 1925 and now a museum, the Asantehene's Palace, built in 1972, the Okomfo Anokye Sword, and the Centre for National Culture, whose Prempeh II Jubilee Museum holds Asante regalia and a reproduction of the Golden Stool. Fort Kumasi, built in 1896 to replace an Asante fort, is now a museum.

The British modernised the city from 1896. The wetlands near the centre were drained in 1905 for the railway linking Accra and Cape Coast, pipe-borne water was developed in the 1920s, and the Central Market was completed in 1925. The University of Science and Technology was established in 1952, and in 1953 Kumasi hosted the Conference of West African Nationalists. In 1945 Maxwell Fry and Jane Drew designed the city's first development plan on the Garden City model of Howard, with green belts, and in the middle of the 20th century Kumasi was called the Garden City of West Africa.

Kumasi is now the second largest city in Ghana, with a population of about 444,000. Its Kejetia Market is the largest in West Africa.

summary: Kumasi, in the forest of Ghana, was founded around 1680 as the capital of the Ashanti Empire. The Aowin sacked it in 1718 and 1719, the British burnt parts of it in 1874 and invaded it again in 1895 and 1896, and it was annexed in 1901. It is now the capital of the Ashanti Region.
references: Gérard Pescheux, Le royaume asante (Ghana): parenté, pouvoir, histoire, XVIIe-XXe siècles (KARTHALA Editions, 2003)
Ivor Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century: The Structure and Evolution of a Political Order (Cambridge University Press, 1989)
notes: START: the history article says 'around 1680 or in the 1680s'; the main article says 'in the 1680s'. I used 1680 with circa true.

CAPITAL DATE: the main article says the city 'rose to prominence in 1695, when it became the capital'; both articles also say it was founded as the capital in the 1680s. I kept both as the articles give them and did not reconcile them.

1874: the main article says 'parts of the city, including the then royal residence, were burnt by the British'; the history article says 'ransacked' in its lead and adds that native carriers were generally blamed for the torching. I used 'burnt parts of' and gave the carriers' blame as the history article does. The word 'destruction in 1874' appears in Freeman's quotation; I used it only in his sense.

1895-96: the history article says 'Kumasi and its nearby villages were destroyed as the British rebuilt the city on the same location', which is garbled; I left it out. The main article says the British took over in 1896; Fort Kumasi is dated 1896 in the main article, and 'modernization began in 1896' with the fort at the centre of town in the history article.

POPULATION: the history article adds 'more than 200,000' (1820) to the main article's estimates; I included it. The present figure 443,981 is from the census, which the article dates to 2021; written without 'as of' as the guide asks (rounded to about 444,000).
LOCKDOWN: the history article's COVID lockdown dates contradict themselves (30 May versus 19/20 April 2020); left out.
Prempeh I's 30 years of exile in the Seychelles are from the main article ('30-year in exile'); 1926 return and 1935 restoration as given there.
Ashanti became a 'formal colony' in 1901 (history article); the main article says the British took Kumasi over in 1896. Both used with their own dates.
The main article's list of Golden Stool legend has a typo ('Athe Ahanti nation'); read as 'the Ashanti nation'.
